extracted.intended_audience: advanced_undergraduate or graduate students and researchers in mathematical logic
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and proofs of central first-order logic metatheorems (soundness, completeness, compactness, enumerability) and accompanying lemmas, model constructions, and decidability results. Contains Henkin-style completeness construction and consequences for finite models and decidability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ ⊢ φ, then Γ |= φ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tells that deductions lead only to logically valid conclusions. Proof idea: show logical axioms are valid and that modus ponens preserves logical implication. Induction on the form of a deduced formula with cases: logical axioms, members of Γ, and modus ponens from earlier formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 25A: Validity of logical axioms
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by considering axiom groups (1–6) and using previous exercises: generalizations of valid formulas are valid; handle equality axioms, quantifier axioms, and substitution-related axioms; reduce to atomic cases and use straightforward semantic checks. This lemma is the base case used in the proof of soundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: If the term t is substitutable for variable x in the wff ϕ, then |=_A ϕ_x^t [s] iff |=_A ϕ [s(x | s(t))].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction on ϕ. Requires the technical notion 't is substitutable for x in ϕ'. Uses Lemma 25B (commutation of substitution in terms and in assignments). Applies to pass from truth of ∀xϕ to truth of instantiated ϕx^t by manipulating assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 25B: Substitution commutes with evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: For any term u, s(u_x^t) = s(x | s(t))(u).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction on terms u. Intuition: performing substitution within a term or changing the assignment to map x to the value of t yield the same evaluated object. Used in the proof of the substitution lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness theorem (Gödel, 1930)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If Γ |= φ then Γ ⊢ φ. (b) Any consistent set of formulas is satisfiable. (Parts (a) and (b) are equivalent.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deeper converse to soundness. Proof given for countable languages via Henkin-style construction: extend language with new constants, add witness sentences, extend to a maximal consistent deductively closed set, build a term model from that set, and (if equality present) quotient by the equality congruence. For uncountable languages modify the cardinalities (add λ many constants, index by ordinals, use Zorn's lemma). The outline lists required properties of the maximal set used to build the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Henkin completeness construction (steps 1–6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete procedure to build a model from a consistent set Γ in a countable language: (1) expand language by adding countably infinite new constants; (2) for each wff ϕ and variable x add a witness sentence ¬∀xϕ → ¬ϕ_x^c using fresh constants, preserving consistency; (3) extend Γ ∪ witness_sentences to a maximally consistent deductively closed set Δ; (4) form structure A with domain = set of terms, interpret predicates/functions so Pt1...tn ∈ Δ iff (t1,...,tn) ∈ P^A, and replace equality by a new predicate E; (5) show E^A is a congruence and form quotient A/E to restore equality; (6) restrict back to the original language to obtain a model of Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: choose fresh constants carefully to avoid clashes; prove consistency at each stage by finiteness and RAA arguments; show Δ is deductively closed; verify by induction that for any ϕ, ϕ ∈ Δ iff A satisfies ϕ* under the identity assignment (where ϕ* replaces = by E); finally use the homomorphism theorem to move from A to A/E. For uncountable languages add λ constants and index witness sentences by ordinals; use Zorn's lemma to get maximal consistent sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If Γ |= φ then some finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ satisfies Γ0 |= φ. (b) If every finite subset of Γ is satisfiable then Γ is satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from completeness and soundness: semantic implication implies syntactic derivability, which is finite. Equivalent proofs avoid deductions (ultraproducts or semantic compactness). Common method to produce infinite models: add sentences λ_k saying 'there are at least k things' and apply compactness to the augmented set to get an infinite model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerability theorem for valid wffs
rubrics_metrics.description: For a reasonable language, the set of valid well-formed formulas can be effectively enumerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define a 'reasonable language' (parameters effectively enumerable and arity relations decidable). The set of logical axioms is decidable, hence the set of deductions (finite sequences) is decidable; enumerate all finite sequences and select those that are deductions — their last members enumerate all validities. Alternative: enumerate tautological consequences of the axioms because the axioms are decidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Reasonable language
rubrics_metrics.description: A language whose set of parameters can be effectively enumerated and such that the two relations {(P,n) | P is an n-place predicate symbol} and {(f,n) | f is an n-place function symbol} are decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: any finite-language (finitely many parameters) is reasonable. A reasonable language must be countable. This condition is used to prove enumerability of validities and to make syntactic checks effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: Logical equivalence from provable biconditional
rubrics_metrics.description: If ⊢ (ϕ ↔ ψ), then ϕ and ψ are logically equivalent (i.e., |= (ϕ ↔ ψ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequence of soundness: provability of equivalence implies semantic equivalence. Related corollary: alphabetic variants are logically equivalent (if ϕ' is an alphabetic variant of ϕ then they are logically equivalent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfiability implies consistency (corollary)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is satisfiable (there exists A and s satisfying every member of Γ), then Γ is consistent (not both φ and ¬φ are provable from Γ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This corollary is equivalent to soundness: satisfiable sets cannot be deductively inconsistent because soundness prevents deriving contradictions true in all models. The textbook invites reader to verify equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerability/Decidability consequences for decidable axiom sets (Corollary 25F & 25G)
rubrics_metrics.description: (25F) If Γ is a decidable set of formulas in a reasonable language then the set of theorems of Γ (i.e., formulas provable from Γ) and {φ | Γ |= φ} are effectively enumerable. (25G) If Γ is decidable and for any sentence σ either Γ |= σ or Γ |= ¬σ, then the set of sentences implied by Γ is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches: enumerate validities and filter those whose premises lie in Γ to enumerate Γ-theorems. If Γ is decidable and complete (for every σ either implied or its negation is implied), then enumerating theorems yields a decision procedure for implication (search for σ or ¬σ among enumerated theorems). Note: general enumerability cannot usually be strengthened to decidability (Church's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 26A: Infinite model from arbitrarily large finite models
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set Σ of sentences has arbitrarily large finite models, then it has an infinite model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sentences λ_k expressing 'there are at least k things' for k ≥ 2. The union Σ ∪ {λ2, λ3, ...} has every finite subset satisfiable by hypothesis, so by compactness the whole set is satisfiable, hence has an infinite model. This method is a standard compactness application to build structures with desired properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences about classes of finite/infinite structures
rubrics_metrics.description: The class of all finite structures (for a fixed language) is not an elementary class (not EC). The class of all infinite structures is not elementary, but it is axiomatizable as Mod{λ2, λ3, ...}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Theorem 26A: if Mod τ were exactly finite structures, then Mod ¬τ would be exactly infinite structures, contradiction. Demonstrates limits of first-order definability of finiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-structure decidability and specifiability (observations and Theorem 26C/D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations: (1) Any finite structure is isomorphic to one with universe {1,...,n}; (2) For finite languages finite structures can be specified by finite strings; (3) Given a finite structure A, a wff ϕ, and an assignment, we can effectively decide whether A satisfies ϕ under that assignment; (4) Given σ and n, one can decide whether σ has an n-element model; (5) The spectrum {n | σ has an n-element model} is decidable. Theorem 26C: For a finite structure A in a finite language, Th(A) is decidable. Theorem 26D: For a finite language, {σ | σ has a finite model} is effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms: evaluate formulas by finite search through the universe (quantifiers trigger n-ary searches); enumerate all n-element structures for fixed n to test existence of n-element models. Use a canonical description δ_A specifying A up to isomorphism to reduce Th(A) to checking semantic implication from δ_A; apply earlier corollaries about decidable theories. Corollary 26E: for finite languages the complement of sentences true in every finite structure is effectively enumerable.
